newsitem.title: YEMEN: Yemen soldier kills eight on election day.
newsitem.headline: Yemen soldier kills eight on election day.

text.p: Five soldiers and three civilians were killed when a soldier opened fire at a polling station before voting started on Sunday in the country's general elections, Yemen's interior minister said.

"Seven people were immediately killed and two were injured when Abdullah Ahmed al-Barkani, a soldier on night duty, suddenly opened fire indiscriminately," minister Hussein Mohammad Arab told a news conference.
"One of the injured died later," he added.
Arab said security officials were continuing investigating the incident but no political motive had been established.
"We were expecting more incidents because some are discontent with holding general elections in Yemen," he said without elaborating.
The minister said one of the victims of the dawn attack in the town of Mukayras in the governorate of Abyan was a member of Yemen's ruling party -- the General Peoples Congress (GPC).

Military police in red berets stood guard as voters, who included elderly men with traditional curved daggers tucked in their belts and women in black veils, began voting at 8 a.m. (0500 GMT) in a race they hope will guarantee enough stability to lure foreign funds into the poor Arab state.
It is the first ballot since a 1994 civil war between northern and southern parts of the country. Polling stations stayed open two hours more than originally planned and closed at 8 p.m. (1700 GMT).

President Ali Abdullah Saleh cast his ballot along with many of Yemen's 4.6 million eligible voters who are choosing from among 2,306 candidates, including 17 women, competing for 301 seats under the banner of 12 parties or as independents.
Voters interviewed in Sanaa seemed hopeful that their ballot slips would make a difference.
Sheikh Mutahid Abdullah al-Saeedi stood outside a polling station on the outskirts of Sanaa and discussed the candidates with other voters.
"I've told people from my village to vote for the person you think is fit to do the job. We have democracy and free elections," al-Saeedi, a community leader, told Reuters.
But a few minutes later he added: "I told them to vote for the congress (the ruling General Peoples)".
"The elections will lead to a better life," said a policeman after election personnel took his thumb print to guarantee he votes only once, a practice throughout the election.
"The Islah Party (junior coalition partner Islamist Islah Party) is good because they say God is greatest. The Congress only steals money and gets fat," said one woman draped in black.
Bilqis al-Hadrany, one of 17 women in the parliamentary race, alleged that the results were predetermined by the government before the contest began.
"There have been a lot of violations. But we did not boycott the elections because we want to push democracy forward," she said.
Minor scuffles were reported at several Sanaa polling stations, but international observers said the election process appeared to be going well.

One election monitor said a decision by the Supreme Election Committee late on Saturday to let 1.4 million registered Yemeni voters cast their ballot even though they had not picked up permanent election cards had raised concerns among some parties.
"There are concerns among some parties that this could lead to manipulation of voting," the observer said.
Voters, many of them illiterate, made their choice with the help of ballot slips bearing the symbols of parties -- from horses and camels to candles and rockets.
Diplomats expect Saleh's GPC and Islah to win a majority.

The main opposition Yemen Socialist Party, some of whose former leaders launched the separatist campaign that sparked the civil war, and three others are boycotting the polls due to alleged irregularities. The government has denied the charges.
Results are expected to start trickling in on Monday afternoon, but final results are only due later in the week.

Diplomats say they are encouraged by Yemen's democratic experiment but add that power ultimately rests in the hands of the president, appointed ministers, the military and security forces loyal to the GPC.
They said the government was trying to boost its democratic image abroad to attract foreign investment and aid to Yemen.
The Republic of Yemen was formed in 1990 by the merger of the conservative north Yemen and the Marxist south.
